To remark means to say something as a comment or observation — usually something brief that you've noticed and want to express out loud (or in writing).

The key idea inside the word is this: you noticed something, and now you're giving voice to that observation. It's the moment when a thought you've had becomes a spoken (or written) comment.

She remarked that the room felt unusually quiet.

This tells us she noticed the quietness, and she said so. It wasn't a long speech. It wasn't a formal argument. It was simply a comment she made — a thought she put into words.

In older, more formal, or literary writing, "remark" can also mean simply to notice or observe something — without necessarily saying anything.

He remarked a slight trembling in her hands.

Here, it means: he noticed a slight trembling. No speech is involved. This usage is rare in everyday modern English, but you might encounter it in classic novels or formal writing, so it's good to know.

In daily life, when people use "remark," they almost always mean the first sense — saying something as a comment.
How to Use It — The Sentence Patterns

Pattern 1: remark + that + (what was said)
This is the most common structure.

He remarked that the food was excellent.
She remarked that the train was running late.
The teacher remarked that the students had improved a lot.

Pattern 2: remark + on/upon + (what was noticed)
Here you use "on" or "upon" to point at the thing being commented about.

Everyone remarked on her beautiful dress.
They remarked on how calm the sea looked.
The doctor remarked upon the patient's quick recovery.

Pattern 3: remark used while quoting speech directly
When a speaker's exact words are given, "remarked" appears after them, like a tag.

"This is quite surprising," she remarked.
"The colour doesn't suit the wall," he remarked.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Remark" carries a sense of casualness and brevity. When someone remarks something, they are not giving a lecture, not making a formal declaration, and not writing an essay. They're simply giving voice to something they noticed — often in a natural, almost offhand way.

There is also often a mild personal quality to it. A remark usually comes from you — from your own observation of something in the moment. It's your small commentary on the world around you.

Compare:

  • He said the painting was beautiful. → Neutral. Just tells us he spoke these words.
  • He remarked that the painting was beautiful. → Tells us he noticed it, was struck by it, and said so as a comment. There's a small but real difference in feel.

This is where the word truly comes alive — by seeing how it sits among its neighbours.

Say — the most plain, neutral word for speaking. It carries no extra meaning. She said it was cold. No implication of noticing, no particular tone.

Comment — very close to "remark." The two are often interchangeable. But "comment" leans slightly more toward responding to something specific or giving an opinion. She commented on the report suggests she is responding to that report directly. She remarked on the report is a touch more spontaneous, more like a passing observation.

Observe — when used in the sense of speaking, "observe" feels a little more formal and analytical than "remark." He observed that crime had increased sounds like a measured, careful statement. He remarked that crime had increased sounds more like something he said in conversation.

Note — often used in formal or written contexts. She noted that the figures were wrong implies careful, deliberate attention. It's more precise and official-sounding than "remark."

Mention — to mention something is to bring it up briefly, often almost in passing, and not necessarily as a comment on something you've noticed. He mentioned he'd been to London is just saying he brought it up. There's less of a "noticing" quality than in "remark."

Point out — to point out is to specifically draw another person's attention to something, often something they might have missed or overlooked. She pointed out that the back door was unlocked. "Remark" doesn't necessarily target the other person's attention that way — it's simply a comment.

To remark is to look at the world — a situation, a person, an event, an idea — notice something about it, and say something brief about what you've noticed. It's the natural human act of turning a quiet observation into a spoken word.

It is not dramatic. It is not lengthy. It is personal and present — something said in the moment, arising from something seen or felt.

She remarked that the stars were especially bright that night.

That single sentence shows you someone who looked up, noticed something, and quietly said so. That is the verb "remark" at its heart.
